newsitem.title: UK: Large UK union steps up pressure for minimum wage.
newsitem.headline: Large UK union steps up pressure for minimum wage.

text.p: Britain's largest trade union Unison, which represents 1.3 million public sector workers, signalled on Monday that it intended to make sure the new Labour government kept its promise to introduce a minimum wage.
Unison asked Prime Minister Tony Blair's two week old administration to set the rate at 4.26 pounds per hour -- the same rate demanded by the Trades Union Congress last year.
"My job is to keep up the pressure for a decent rate which will really make a difference to the army of workers on poverty pay," said General Secretary Rodney Bickerstaffe.

"Many of those who oppose the minimum wage are high earners, out of touch with the real-life struggle of surviving on poverty pay. Let them tell these UNISON members why they should not be paid a fair wage for a fair day's work."

The report said the severity and extent of poverty had increased rapidly during 18 years of Conservative government and more than 5.6 million people -- one in four workers aged 18 or more -- were now paid less than 4.26 an hour.
In contrast, official figures show average hourly earnings for employees in Britain are at 7.36 pounds.
Britain first had a minimum wage in 1909, introduced through the Wages Council.
The Conservatives, ousted on May 1, abolished the Council in 1993 for all but agricultural workers, arguing that a compulsory floor on pay levels was stifling job creation.

Labour, which has its roots in the trade union movement, places greater emphasis on employee rights and argues that most major industrial nations, such as the U.S. and Japan, have minimum pay levels without damaging employment.
The UNISON report argued that increases in the U.S. minimum wage had reduced inequality there as well as in France.
It said that a minimum wage of 4.26 percent hour would benefit more women -- 3.46 million -- than men -- 1.74 million.
Just over half the affected workers would be part-time employees.
Unison said that while there was no detailed breakdown on pay levels for different ethnic groups, there was evidence that black workers were more likely to work in sectors which pay low wages.
But if the minimum wage were set at 3.20 stg, only eight percent of the workforce or 1.82 million would benefit from it, the report said.
British business leaders have said that a minimum wage of 4.26 pounds per hour would be too high and could cost jobs.

The Confederation of British Industry has said that a national minimum wage of 3.0 pounds per hour would have only a limited impact on employment provided there was no general attempt by higher paid workers to restore pay differentials.

The new government is establishing a Low Pay Commission to advise on the level of the minimum wage and newspapers have reported that the Commission will be headed by Peter Jarvis, chief executive of brewery and Leisure Group Whitbread PLC.
This has already provoked concerns from the unions.

Bill Morris, General secretary of the giant Transport and General Workers Union, warned Labour on Friday not to "put Dracula in charge of the blood bank," but did not comment specifically on reports about Jarvis.
Morris said the party should appoint a chairman of the minimum wage commission who understood the issues. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
